etymology: From boogie-woogie, the rolling, eight-to-the-bar piano blues style named in Pinetop Smith’s "Pinetop’s Boogie Woogie" (1928), itself of uncertain origin (perhaps from West African words for dance or from boogie, a rent party). In 1970s funk and disco slang to boogie meant to dance energetically, and also simply to leave in a hurry ("Let’s boogie"). The decade was full of it: "Boogie Fever" (1976), "Boogie Oogie Oogie" (1978), "Boogie Wonderland" (1979).
biblical_def: To boogie is to dance with abandon — on a 1970s disco floor, at a wedding, in the kitchen — or, in another sense, to get going: "We’d better boogie or we’ll miss the game." The Christian observation: Scripture is not afraid of the dance and not naive about it. It commands joyful dancing before God: "Let them praise his name in the dance: let them sing praises unto him with the timbrel and harp" (Psa 149:3); "Praise him with the timbrel and dance" (Psa 150:4). When the prodigal came home, his brother "heard musick and dancing" (Luk 15:25), and the father was the one who had ordered the party. God turns mourning into dancing (Psa 30:11). But the same Scripture records another dance. At the foot of Sinai, Israel "sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play" around a golden calf, and when Moses "saw the calf, and the dancing" he broke the tablets of the law (Exo 32:6, 19). The difference is not in the feet but in the object. Is the dance a thanksgiving to God, in the company of His people, with the body kept honorable? Or is it a celebration of the self and its appetites, in the dark, with the old revellings Peter warned against (1Pe 4:3)? The 1970s gave the word mostly to the second kind of floor. A Christian family can reclaim it: boogie at the wedding, boogie in the kitchen with the little ones, and remember Whose music it is.
webster_summary: 1970s slang (from 1920s boogie-woogie) for dancing energetically, or for leaving quickly — Scripture commands the joyful dance of praise (Psa 149:3) and warns of the dance around the golden calf (Exo 32:19).
webster_full: BOOGIE, v.i. (Boomer slang, 1970s) 1. To dance energetically, especially to rock, funk, or disco. 2. To leave; to get moving: "Let’s boogie." n. 1. Boogie-woogie music. 2. A dance; a party.
From boogie-woogie (1928), a blues piano style with a driving repeated bass figure.
Decode for families: "boogie board" (a short surf board, 1971) is the same word, and the most innocent use of it.
scriptures: Let them praise his name in the dance: let them sing praises unto him with the timbrel and harp.
Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs.
Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing.
Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;

And it came to pass, as soon as he came nigh unto the camp, that he saw the calf, and the dancing: and Moses' anger waxed hot, and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount.
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
corruption_summary: The 1970s gave boogie to the dance of the self and the night; Scripture commands joyful dancing in praise and celebration, and judges the dance around the golden calf.
corruption_paragraphs: The disco floor of 1977 and the camp beneath Sinai have something in common: both were festivals of the self. Israel made a god it could see and dance around; the disco made the dancer the god, lit from below, on display. Both ended the same way — in excess and, for many, in ruin. Peter names the old life: "lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings" (1Pe 4:3). That is what the night club sells.

But Christians who flee the club should not flee joy. The Psalms call God’s people to dance before Him, and the Lord’s parable of the prodigal ends with music and dancing in the father’s house (Luk 15:25). The answer to bad dancing is good dancing — at weddings, at harvest, at homecomings, with the generations together and the Lord thanked.
roots_summary: Uncertain (perhaps West African dance words) → 1920s boogie-woogie (piano blues; Pinetop Smith, 1928) → 1970s boogie (to dance; to leave).
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; perhaps from West African words for dancing, or Black American boogie, a rent party
1928: "Pinetop’s Boogie Woogie" names the piano style
1940s: boogie-woogie swing and jump blues
1970s funk and disco: boogie — to dance; "let’s boogie" — let’s go
Hebrew machol — dance, dancing (Psa 149:3; Psa 30:11)
usage: "At the wedding Grandpa said, ‘Watch this,’ and boogied. We are still recovering."
Let them praise his name in the dance (Psa 149:3).
Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing (Psa 30:11).

etymology: Short for discothèque, French for a record library, the name taken by Paris nightclubs of the 1940s–50s where records replaced live bands. In the 1970s disco named both the clubs and the music — a pulsing four-on-the-floor dance style out of Black, Latino, and gay clubs in New York and Philadelphia — and the whole scene: mirror balls, polyester, cocaine. Studio 54 opened in April 1977; Saturday Night Fever (December 1977) took disco mainstream; and "Disco Demolition Night" at Chicago’s Comiskey Park (July 12, 1979) marked the backlash.
biblical_def: Disco was the music and nightlife of the late 1970s: thumping dance records, mirrored balls, glittering clothes, John Travolta strutting down a Brooklyn street, and clubs like Studio 54 where the famous danced until dawn. Most Boomers either loved it or burned their records in protest. The Christian observation: the music itself can be a cheerful thing — a strong beat and a happy melody are no sin — but the disco culture was a temple of the night, and Scripture describes it with uncanny precision. Isaiah: "the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands" (Isa 5:12). That was the club: music and wine and no thought of God. Peter names the rest: "lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries" (1Pe 4:3). Studio 54 was notorious for its drugs and sexual excess, and within a few years the disco world was devastated by addiction and disease. Paul’s counsel was written for exactly such a city: "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness" (Rom 13:13). The children of the day do not need the mirror ball. A grandparent who danced to the Bee Gees can laugh about the leisure suit and still tell a grandchild the truth: the night always promises more than it pays.
webster_summary: 1970s slang (from French discothèque) for the dance clubs, the pulsing dance music, and the nightlife scene of 1975–79 — the music "in their feasts" with no regard for the work of the LORD (Isa 5:12).
webster_full: DISCO, n. (1960s; Boomer era, chiefly 1974–79) 1. A nightclub for dancing to recorded music; a discotheque. 2. Popular dance music of the 1970s, with a steady four-beat rhythm, lush strings, and soul vocals. v.i. To dance to such music.
From French discothèque (record library), on the pattern of bibliothèque.
Decode for families: "Disco Sucks" T-shirts (1979) were the backlash; ask Grandpa which side he was on.
scriptures: Isa 5:12
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
Exo 32:6
And they rose up early on the morrow, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.
Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs.
corruption_summary: Disco culture made the night club a temple of self-display, drugs, and sexual excess; Scripture calls the children of the day to walk honestly and gives music and dancing back to the praise of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Disco began in the underground clubs of New York as music for people who felt shut out of mainstream life, and its joy was real. But it was a joy that ran on the night and its pleasures, and by the time it reached Studio 54 it had become a cathedral of excess: velvet ropes, celebrity, cocaine on the tables, sex in the balconies. The music’s relentless four-beat pulse was designed to keep dancers on the floor for hours, and the drugs helped. Many who lived that life did not survive the next decade.

Scripture does not tell Christians to hate a beat. It tells them to "walk honestly, as in the day" (Rom 13:13) and to refuse the revellings of their former life (1Pe 4:3). The question is not whether a song is danceable but whether it is drawing a person into the day or into the night. Psalm 150 ends with cymbals, timbrels, and dance — and with the line that reorders every dance floor: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD."
roots_summary: Greek diskos (a disk) + thēkē (a case) → French discothèque (record library; nightclub, 1940s–50s) → 1960s disco → 1970s music and scene.
roots_lines: Greek diskos — a quoit, a disk; thēkē — a case, a repository
French discothèque — record library; Paris nightclubs, 1940s–50s
1970s: disco music from New York and Philadelphia clubs
April 1977: Studio 54 opens; December 1977: Saturday Night Fever
July 12, 1979: Disco Demolition Night, Comiskey Park, Chicago
usage: "Grandma has a disco ball in the attic. She says it was for a church youth skate night. We believe her mostly."
They regard not the work of the LORD (Isa 5:12).
Let us walk honestly, as in the day (Rom 13:13).

etymology: In 1960s–70s African-American and funk slang, get down meant to dance with abandon, to let loose, to enjoy oneself fully, or to get serious about something ("get down to business"). James Brown’s shouts made it famous, KC and the Sunshine Band’s "Get Down Tonight" (No. 1, 1975) made it national, and Kool & the Gang’s "Get Down On It" (1981) kept it going.
biblical_def: To get down is to let loose and enjoy yourself completely — to dance hard, to party, to throw yourself into the moment. "Everybody get down!" The Christian observation: the phrase names a whole-hearted joy, and Scripture is not against whole-hearted joy; it is for it, and it knows where to find it. David got down before the ark, dancing "with all his might," and when his wife Michal sneered at the king acting so undignified, he answered: "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight" (2Sa 6:22). That is joy that does not care how it looks because it is aimed at God. Nehemiah told a weeping people to go and feast, "for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). The Psalmist knew the source: "in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore" (Psa 16:11). Paul commands it outright: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice" (Php 4:4). The funk lyric meant something else — a night of pleasure, often a sexual one. Scripture does not compete with that by being dull; it competes by being deeper. The joy of the Lord is the only joy you can get down to without regret in the morning. A father who laughs loud, sings loud in church, and dances with his daughter at her wedding is showing his children that faith is not a frown.
webster_summary: 1960s–70s funk slang for dancing hard and enjoying oneself fully ("Get Down Tonight," 1975) — whole-hearted joy that Scripture locates in God’s presence (Psa 16:11) and models in David dancing with all his might (2Sa 6:22).
webster_full: GET DOWN, v. phr. (African-American and funk slang, 1960s–70s; Boomer era) 1. To dance energetically; to let oneself go. 2. To enjoy oneself fully; to party. 3. To get serious; to apply oneself ("get down to business").
Decode for families: in 1975 lyrics, get down tonight usually meant more than dancing. In a grandparent’s mouth today it usually means dancing.
scriptures: And I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight: and of the maidservants which thou hast spoken of, of them shall I be had in honour.
Neh 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Php 4:4
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
corruption_summary: The funk anthem sought whole-hearted joy in a night of pleasure; Scripture offers a deeper whole-hearted joy in God’s presence, with no regrets in the morning.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of 1970s pop music was an argument that joy is found in the body, the night, and the moment. "Get down tonight" was its motto. The argument persuaded a generation, and the morning-after cost was paid in broken marriages and broken lives. The Christian should not answer that argument with gloom, as though God were against joy. He should answer it with a better joy.

That better joy has a shape. It is "in thy presence" (Psa 16:11), so it does not fade when the music stops. It is "of the LORD" (Neh 8:10), so it is strength, not weakness. And it is unembarrassed: David danced in front of everyone and did not care what Michal thought (2Sa 6:22). The father in the parable did not send his returning son to a quiet room; "they began to be merry" (Luk 15:24). The gospel is the best reason in the universe to get down.
roots_summary: Get (Old Norse geta) + down → 1960s–70s AAVE / funk get down (dance, let loose) → "Get Down Tonight" (1975).

James Brown’s stage shouts popularize the phrase

Hebrew simchah — joy, gladness (Neh 8:10; Psa 16:11)

The joy of the LORD is your strength (Neh 8:10).
In thy presence is fulness of joy (Psa 16:11).

etymology: Bump is an imitative word for a knock or swelling (sixteenth century; Webster 1828: a swelling; to strike, to thump). The Bump was a disco dance of 1974–75 in which partners knocked hips (or other parts) together on the beat; it spawned hit records ("The Bump," Kenny, 1974; "Do the Bump"). Earlier, burlesque used bump and grind for a stripper’s hip thrusts. Later slang added bump for a dose of cocaine and for bringing an online post back to the top.
biblical_def: The Bump was a 1970s dance: partners side by side, bumping hips in time to the music — silly, flirtatious, and briefly everywhere. The word’s neighbors are less innocent: bump and grind (burlesque) and, later, a bump of cocaine. The Christian observation: the dance itself was mostly goofy fun, but it belonged to a decade that was teaching young people to treat the body as a toy, and Scripture speaks to the body with great seriousness and great dignity. "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s" (1Co 6:19–20). The body is not a toy, a commodity, or a weapon; it is a temple and an offering: "present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service" (Rom 12:1). That does not forbid play. Children bump into each other in games; husbands and wives laugh and dance together; there is "a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4). It does forbid making the body a stage for lust, and it forbids the other bump — the drug that enslaves the temple to a chemical. A family can laugh at a grandparent’s attempt at the Bump and still teach the children the truth Paul wrote to a city famous for its night life: you are not your own.
webster_summary: 1970s disco dance (1974–75) in which partners bumped hips on the beat; neighbor to burlesque’s bump and grind and later drug slang — set by Scripture against the body as the temple of the Holy Ghost (1Co 6:19).
webster_full: BUMP, n. (Boomer slang, 1974–75) The Bump, a disco dance in which partners rhythmically knock hips together. v.i. To dance the Bump. Related: bump and grind (burlesque, 1930s); bump (later drug slang), a small dose of cocaine.
Webster (1828) — BUMP, noun [Latin bombus, and Eng. pomp., from swelling, thrusting out.] 1. A swelling or protuberance. 2. A thump; a heavy blow.
Decode for families: if your teenager "bumps" a post, it means moving it back to the top of a feed. Different decade, different bump.
scriptures: What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
Rom 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;
corruption_summary: The Bump was mostly silly fun inside a decade that taught the young to treat the body as a toy or a stage; Scripture calls the body a temple, bought with a price, to be presented to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The disco dances of the mid-1970s — the Bump, the Hustle, the Bus Stop — were cheerful line and partner dances, closer to a square dance than to anything sinister. But they sat on a continuum that ran quickly from flirtation to display, and the decade did not stop at the cheerful end. The burlesque bump and grind moved from back-alley theaters toward the mainstream, and the drug bump moved from the margins into the clubs. A word’s neighbors are worth knowing.

Paul’s word to the Corinthians (1Co 6:19–20) is the Christian charter for the body. It is not evil; it is holy. It is not mine; it is God’s. It is not for sale; it has been bought. That truth protects a young person far better than a list of forbidden dances: whatever you do with your body, do it as one who carries a temple around.
roots_summary: Imitative bump (a knock, a swelling; 16th c.) → 1930s burlesque bump and grind → 1974–75 disco dance the Bump → later drug and internet senses.

etymology: From Dutch husselen / hutselen, to shake or toss (seventeenth century), whence English hustle, to shake together, push, or crowd (Webster 1828). American slang gave it two careers: (1) to swindle or obtain by aggressive or dishonest means, with hustler for a con man or gambler (later nineteenth and early twentieth century; The Hustler, 1961); (2) energetic effort, "hustle" in sports. In 1975 Van McCoy’s "The Hustle" (No. 1) named a disco line and partner dance that became the signature dance of the era.
biblical_def: In Boomer memory the Hustle is a disco dance — Van McCoy’s 1975 hit and the line dance everyone learned at weddings. But the word has a longer and darker life: to hustle is to con, to swindle, to get money by fast talk, and a hustler is a pool shark, a scam artist, or worse. In sports it means effort and drive, and today’s "hustle culture" praises working without rest. The Christian observation: Scripture sorts the meanings cleanly. The swindling hustle is condemned: "The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death" (Pro 21:6); "Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase" (Pro 13:11). The thief is told to become a worker: "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28). Honest effort is commended: "the hand of the diligent maketh rich" (Pro 10:4), and "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23). But hustle culture, which treats rest as weakness, runs into the fourth commandment and into Psalm 127: it is vain to rise up early and sit up late. A father can teach his son to hustle on the field and at the job, never to hustle a neighbor, and to rest on the Lord’s Day as a confession that God, not his hustle, holds the world together.
webster_summary: From 1828 hustle (to shake, to crowd) to American slang for swindling, for energetic effort, and the 1975 disco dance — Scripture condemns the con (Pro 21:6), commends diligent labor (Pro 10:4), and limits striving with rest.
webster_full: HUSTLE, n. (Boomer era) 1. The Hustle — a disco line and partner dance popularized by Van McCoy’s "The Hustle" (1975). 2. A swindle or racket. 3. Energetic activity; drive. v. To swindle; to sell aggressively; to work or play with great energy. Hustler, a con artist or gambler.
Webster (1828) — HUSTLE, verb intransitive hus’l. To shake together in confusion; to push or crowd.
Decode for families: "hustle" on a coach’s lips is praise; on a detective’s it is a charge; on a 2020s influencer’s it is a lifestyle. Ask which one is meant.
scriptures: Pro 21:6
The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death.
Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
Eph 4:28
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Pro 10:4
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
corruption_summary: Hustle blurs the con, the honest effort, and the restless striving; Scripture condemns treasure by a lying tongue, commends the diligent hand, and binds all labor to rest.
corruption_paragraphs: American English has made a hero of the hustler. The con man in the movies is charming; the street hustler is a survivor; the startup founder "hustles" his way to a billion. The word smuggles admiration for cunning into the vocabulary of work. Scripture refuses the admiration. Proverbs calls ill-gotten gain "a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death" (Pro 21:6). Paul tells the thief not merely to stop but to start working so he can give (Eph 4:28) — the exact reversal of the hustler’s life.

The newer hustle culture is subtler and more respectable: work every waking hour, sleep when you’re dead, rest is for the weak. It sounds like diligence, and Scripture praises diligence (Pro 10:4). But Scripture also commands rest, and the man who will not rest is telling God he does not trust Him. Teach children to work hard; teach them to stop.

etymology: Jam, an informal improvised performance by jazz musicians, is recorded from the late 1920s; jam session appears by the early 1930s in swing-era usage. Rock musicians of the 1960s took it over — long improvised jams were a hallmark of the Grateful Dead, Cream, and the Allman Brothers — and to jam and a jam became common words for any informal music-making (and later, in Gen X and later slang, for a favorite song: "this is my jam").
biblical_def: A jam session is an informal gathering of musicians who play together without a script, trading solos and building on each other’s ideas — in a 1930s Harlem club, a 1969 rehearsal barn, or a basement with three teenagers and a drum kit. The Christian observation: Scripture is full of music, and a good deal of it sounds like a holy jam. David organized the Levites into bands, and the Chronicler records the musicians "that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning" (1Ch 25:7) — skilled, trained, and offered to God. The Psalmist asks for both skill and joy: "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3). Psalm 150 calls in the whole band: trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, strings, organ, loud cymbals, high sounding cymbals. And the early church’s gatherings had a participatory, every-member quality: "when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm" (1Co 14:26), with the governing rule, "Let all things be done unto edifying." Paul tells the church to teach and admonish "one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord" (Col 3:16). The jam session’s gifts — listening to one another, building on another’s idea, making something together that none could make alone — are body-of-Christ gifts. A family that sings and plays together on a Sunday evening has the best kind of jam session.
webster_summary: Swing-era jazz slang (early 1930s), revived by 1960s rock, for an informal improvised gathering of musicians — a shared music-making Scripture honors when skill and joy are offered to God (Psa 33:3; Col 3:16).
webster_full: JAM SESSION, n. (swing-era slang, early 1930s; revived in 1960s rock) An informal gathering at which musicians improvise together. Also jam (n. and v.). Later: my jam, a favorite song.

Webster (1828) — SESSION, noun [Latin sessio , from sedeo . See Set .] 1. A sitting or being placed; as the ascension of Christ and his session at the right hand of God. 2. The actual sitting of a court, council, legislature, etc.; or the actual assembly of the members of these o rany similar body for the transaction of business. Thus we say, the court is now in session , meaning that the members are assembled for business.
Decode for families: the Presbyterian session (the elders’ court) and the jam session share only a Latin root — both are a "sitting together."
scriptures: Psa 33:3
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
So the number of them, with their brethren that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning, was two hundred fourscore and eight.
Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp.
How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: A largely wholesome word; the rock jam culture often surrounded it with drugs, but the practice itself — skilled, shared, improvised music — is something Scripture celebrates when it is offered to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1960s jam culture had a shadow: the long improvised jam became associated with drug-fueled concerts, and some bands treated the jam as a kind of trance. That shadow belongs to the setting, not to the music. Improvisation is a skill, built on years of practice, and the best jazz and rock musicians brought real discipline to it. Psalm 33:3 asks for exactly that: skill and loudness together.

The church has its own version, and it can recover it. Congregational singing, hymn sings, families making music at home — these are jam sessions in the oldest sense, and they knit people together. Paul’s rule is the right one for any jam: "Let all things be done unto edifying" (1Co 14:26).
roots_summary: Jam (1920s jazz, an improvised performance; perhaps from jam, to press together) + Latin sessio (a sitting) → jam session (early 1930s) → 1960s rock jams.

Late 1920s jazz slang: jam — an improvised performance
Early 1930s: jam session
Latin sessio — a sitting (see Session)
1960s rock: extended jams; 1990s–: "this is my jam"
usage: "Grandpa brought his old guitar to Thanksgiving and we had a jam session in the living room. Mostly hymns and one Beatles song."
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise (Psa 33:3).
Every one of you hath a psalm (1Co 14:26).

etymology: From the phonograph record: a needle that tracks well is "in the groove." Swing-era jazz musicians of the 1930s used in the groove for playing smoothly and well, in perfect rhythm, and groovy followed in 1937; the 1960s counterculture revived both, and in the groove broadened to mean performing at one’s best, in form, settled into a rhythm. Madonna’s "Into the Groove" (1985) carried it into the next generation.
biblical_def: To be in the groove is to be performing smoothly and well, at ease in a rhythm — a musician who is locked in with the band, a worker who has found his pace, an athlete in top form. The Christian observation: Scripture describes the godly life with a similar image, and it is worth asking what groove a person is in. The righteous man of Psalm 1 "shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season" (Psa 1:3) — a life in God’s rhythm, fruitful because rooted. Craftsmanship in the groove is a gift of God: Bezaleel was filled "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship" (Exo 31:3). Diligent skill is honored: "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). But a groove can also be a rut. The same phonograph needle can be stuck, playing one bar over and over; a man can settle into a groove of sin as easily as a groove of virtue. The source of the right groove is union with Christ: "He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing" (Joh 15:5). The Christian’s best groove is the rhythm of the means of grace — Word, prayer, Lord’s Day, sacraments — kept week by week until it becomes second nature.
webster_summary: Swing-era slang (1930s, from the phonograph needle) for performing smoothly and well, revived in the 1960s — the rhythm of the fruitful tree of Psa 1:3, which comes from abiding in Christ (Joh 15:5).
webster_full: IN THE GROOVE, phr. (swing-era slang, 1930s; Boomer revival 1960s) Performing smoothly, skillfully, and in good rhythm; in top form; settled into a satisfying routine. Related: groovy (1937; 1960s).

Webster (1828) — GROOVE, noun groov. 1. A furrow, channel, or long hollow cut by a tool. Among joiners, a channel in the edge of a molding, style or rail. 2. Among miners, a shaft or pit sunk into the earth.
Decode for families: a groove can be a rhythm or a rut. Teach both words.
scriptures: Psa 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
corruption_summary: A wholesome phrase for skill and rhythm; the only caution is that a groove can be a rut, and the right rhythm comes from abiding in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in in the groove; it describes a good thing. Skill, practice, rhythm, and ease in one’s work are gifts, and Scripture honors the craftsman (Exo 31:3) and the diligent man (Pro 22:29). If anything, the phrase is a reminder that excellence is usually the fruit of repetition: the musician in the groove has played those scales ten thousand times.

The spiritual application is the same. Many Christians want to be in the groove spiritually without the repetition — the daily Bible reading, the weekly worship, the steady prayer. But the tree of Psalm 1 bears fruit because it is planted and stays planted. The groove of grace is cut by faithful repetition, and Christ is the One who makes it fruitful (Joh 15:5).
roots_summary: Middle Dutch groeve (a furrow) → English groove → the phonograph record’s groove → 1930s swing in the groove, groovy (1937) → 1960s revival.
roots_lines: Middle Dutch groeve — a furrow, a ditch; Old English græf — a grave, a trench
English groove — a channel cut by a tool (1828)
Early 20th c.: the spiral groove of the phonograph record
1930s swing: in the groove — playing well; 1937 groovy
1960s counterculture revival; 1985, "Into the Groove"
usage: "By October Grandpa says he’s finally in the groove with his garden — just in time for frost."
Like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season (Psa 1:3).
Without me ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5).

etymology: From rap, to talk freely and at length, African-American slang of the 1960s (perhaps from the older rap, to utter sharply or suddenly — Webster 1828 gives "to utter with sudden violence"), + session. Rap session, an open, informal group discussion, appears in the late 1960s and was everywhere in the early 1970s: campus dorms, church youth groups, encounter groups, and the consciousness-raising circles of the women’s movement. Rap as a music genre came later (late 1970s).
biblical_def: A rap session was a 1970s group conversation: everyone sitting in a circle, talking openly about feelings, problems, politics, or faith, with no set agenda. Youth groups had them; therapy groups ran on them; churches tried them. The Christian observation: the rap session reached for something Scripture commends — honest talk among friends — and also illustrates something Scripture warns about. The commendation: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (Pro 27:17). "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established" (Pro 15:22). And in Malachi’s day, "they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him" (Mal 3:16) — God Himself listened in on that rap session. The warning: talk is not the same as wisdom, and much talk is often the opposite. "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Pro 10:19). Many 1970s rap sessions became exercises in sharing feelings with no anchor — every opinion equal, no one in charge, no Word on the table. That is the folly of Pro 18:2: "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself." The best Christian rap session has an open Bible in the middle of the circle, a mature believer guiding it, and the rule of James: "swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19).
webster_summary: Late-1960s–70s slang (from AAVE rap, to talk freely) for an open, informal group discussion — honest talk Scripture commends when it sharpens (Pro 27:17) and warns against when it is many words without the Word (Pro 10:19).
webster_full: RAP SESSION, n. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–70s) An informal, open group discussion, especially one for airing personal problems or views. From rap (v., 1960s AAVE), to talk freely, to converse.

Webster (1828) — RAP, verb transitive To strike with a quick blow; to knock. with one great peal they rap the door. To rap out, to utter with sudden violence; as, to rap out an oath. [In the popular language of the United States, it is often pronounced rip, to rip out an oath; Latin crepo.]
Decode for families: the youth-group "rap session" of 1972 is the "small group" of 2022. The question is the same: is there a Bible in the circle?
scriptures: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
corruption_summary: The rap session sought honest community through open talk but often made feelings the authority and words the goal; Scripture commends counsel among the godly and warns that in the multitude of words there wanteth not sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The rap session was the liturgy of the therapeutic 1970s. Its unspoken creed was that talking about a problem is solving it, that every feeling deserves expression, and that no one in the circle may judge anyone else. Some good came of it — people who had never spoken honestly found that they could. But much of it was talk without truth. Proverbs warns that the fool’s delight is not understanding but self-display (Pro 18:2), and a circle where everyone discovers his heart and no one hears God’s Word is a circle of fools, however kind.

The church’s version is older and better. Malachi’s faithful remnant spoke often to one another, and the LORD listened (Mal 3:16). Their talk was anchored in the fear of the LORD. A family or a youth group that talks honestly around the Scriptures, with elders guiding and the young swift to hear, has the real thing.
roots_summary: Middle English rappen (to strike) → rap (to utter sharply; 1828) → 1960s AAVE rap (to talk freely) + session → late-1960s rap session.
roots_lines: Middle English rappen — to strike, to knock (imitative)
Rap — to utter suddenly or sharply; to rap out an oath (1828)
1960s AAVE: rap — to talk, to converse freely
Late 1960s–70s: rap session — open group discussion; consciousness-raising groups
Late 1970s: rap as a music genre (a later, separate development)
usage: "Grandpa says the 1972 youth-group rap sessions were where he first heard the gospel explained plainly."
Iron sharpeneth iron (Pro 27:17).
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin (Pro 10:19).

etymology: From the film star Humphrey Bogart (1899–1957), famous for the cigarette that dangled from his lip and was rarely passed. In late-1960s drug culture to bogart meant to hog a shared marijuana cigarette, from the Fraternity of Man’s song "Don’t Bogart Me" (1968; "Don’t bogart that joint, my friend, pass it over to me"), featured on the Easy Rider soundtrack (1969). The verb broadened to mean to keep something greedily for oneself ("Don’t bogart the popcorn"), and in some regions to bully or muscle in.
biblical_def: To bogart something is to hog it — to keep for yourself what is meant to be shared. The word was born in a drug circle, where a joint was supposed to go around, and the man who held on to it was told not to bogart it. It now applies to anything: the popcorn, the remote, the last slice of pizza. The Christian observation: the setting of the word is not innocent — the believer’s body is "the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1Co 6:19), and the drug circle is no place for it — but the sin the word names is real and common, and Scripture speaks to it directly. Bogarting is selfishness in small things. "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:4). Proverbs describes the economics of generosity: "There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself" (Pro 11:24–25). The Lord Jesus said "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (Act 20:35), and Paul tells the rich to be "ready to distribute, willing to communicate" (1Ti 6:18). A child who learns not to bogart the toys is learning the first lesson of Christian charity; a father who passes the last slice to his son without being asked is teaching it.
webster_summary: Late-1960s drug-culture slang (from Humphrey Bogart’s dangling cigarette; "Don’t Bogart Me," 1968) for hogging what should be shared — a small selfishness Scripture answers: "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (Act 20:35).
webster_full: BOGART, v.t. (Boomer slang, late 1960s) 1. Originally, to keep a shared marijuana cigarette too long without passing it. 2. To hog; to keep greedily for oneself. "Don’t bogart the chips." 3. (regional) To bully; to force one’s way.
From Humphrey Bogart (1899–1957), the film actor, whose cigarette famously hung from his lip.
Decode for families: the word’s first home was a drug circle. Its common modern meaning is just "hog."
scriptures: Php 2:4
Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.
That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;
What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?
corruption_summary: Bogart was born in the drug circle and names hoarding what should be shared; Scripture guards the body as a temple and answers the small selfishness with the blessedness of giving.
corruption_paragraphs: The word carries a small irony. In the drug culture, the one sin you could commit was not taking the drug but keeping too much of it. That is a fair picture of how sin works: it creates its own little rules of fairness while breaking God’s. The Christian father need not dwell on the joint; he should simply be honest that the word’s first home was a place his children should not go, and that their bodies belong to the Lord (1Co 6:19).

The sin the word names, though, deserves attention, because it is so ordinary. Most selfishness is not grand; it is the remote, the front seat, the last cookie. Paul’s command in Php 2:4 is the household cure: look also on the things of others. A family that practices passing the plate before taking from it is practicing the gospel in miniature.
roots_summary: Humphrey Bogart (1899–1957) → late-1960s drug slang bogart (hog a joint) → "Don’t Bogart Me" (1968), Easy Rider (1969) → general "to hog."
roots_lines: Humphrey Bogart, film actor, famous for a dangling, unshared cigarette
1968: the Fraternity of Man, "Don’t Bogart Me"
1969: the song on the Easy Rider soundtrack spreads the verb
1970s–present: bogart — to hog anything
Greek koinōnikos — "willing to communicate," ready to share (1Ti 6:18)
usage: "Quit bogarting the popcorn." "Where did you learn that word?" "Grandpa."
Look not every man on his own things (Php 2:4).
It is more blessed to give than to receive (Act 20:35).

etymology: From flake, a thin scale or chip (Webster 1828 has the noun of snow and other flakes), whence to flake off, to peel away. Mid-twentieth-century American slang used flake out for collapsing or falling asleep from exhaustion; baseball slang of the 1950s called an eccentric player a flake or flaky, and by the 1960s–70s flaky meant unreliable and to flake (out) meant to fail to show up or follow through. A flake is someone you cannot count on.
biblical_def: To flake out once meant to collapse from exhaustion; to Boomers and their children it mostly means to bail — to not show up, to forget, to drop a commitment at the last minute. "He said he’d help me move and then flaked." A flake is a person you cannot count on. The Christian observation: Scripture places reliability near the center of godly character, and it describes the flake vividly. "Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint" (Pro 25:19) — you lean on him at the worst moment and he gives way. The man who may dwell in God’s holy hill is the one who "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" (Psa 15:4) — he keeps his word even when it costs him. Our Lord asked for plain, dependable speech: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). His own disciples flaked on Him in His hour of need: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" (Mat 26:40). And He warned that discipleship admits no flaking: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luk 9:62). The comfort is that the Lord who was flaked on is Himself utterly faithful — He forgave Peter and restored him. A father teaches reliability best by being reliable: showing up to the game, keeping the promised fishing trip, being home when he said he would be.
webster_summary: Mid-20th-c. slang (from flake, to peel away) for collapsing from exhaustion, and in Boomer and later usage for failing to show or follow through — the unfaithful man who is like a broken tooth in time of trouble (Pro 25:19).
webster_full: FLAKE OUT, v.i. (American slang, mid-20th c.; Boomer era–present) 1. To collapse or fall asleep from exhaustion. 2. To fail to show up or keep a commitment; to back out. Flake, n., an unreliable or eccentric person; flaky, adj.
Webster (1828) — FLAKE, verb intransitive To break or separate in layers; to peel or scale off. We more usually say, to flake off.
Decode for families: "don’t be a flake" is one of the most useful sentences a parent can teach.
scriptures: Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
And he cometh unto the disciples, and findeth them asleep, and saith unto Peter, What, could ye not watch with me one hour?
Luk 9:62
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Flaking treats commitments as provisional and one’s word as cheap; Scripture makes faithfulness to one’s word a mark of the man who dwells in God’s holy hill.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1970s celebrated spontaneity and distrusted commitment, and the word flake grew up in that soil. If you keep your options open and follow your feelings, you will flake; it is built in. The modern world has made it worse: a text message lets a person cancel at the last minute without facing anyone. The flake rarely thinks of himself as a liar, but Scripture treats an unkept word as a serious matter. The man of Psalm 15 keeps his oath even to his own hurt.

The deepest answer to flakiness is the faithfulness of God. "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." The disciples flaked in Gethsemane (Mat 26:40), and Christ did not flake on them; He went to the cross. A Christian who has been loved by a God who never backs out learns to keep his own word — to show up, to follow through, to finish the furrow (Luk 9:62).
roots_summary: Old Norse flakna (to flake off) → English flake (a thin scale; 1828) → mid-20th-c. flake out (to collapse) → 1950s baseball flaky → 1960s–70s flake (unreliable person).
roots_lines: Old Norse flakna — to flake off, to split
English flake — a small loose piece, as of snow (see Flake)
Mid-20th c.: flake out — to collapse, to fall asleep
1950s baseball: flake, flaky — an eccentric player
1960s–70s: flaky — unreliable; to flake — to fail to show
usage: "Grandpa has never flaked on a promise in his life. That’s why we believe him about the fish."
He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not (Psa 15:4).
Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth (Pro 25:19).

etymology: From trip, a drug experience and, by extension, any state of mind or preoccupation (mid-1960s: "a power trip," "an ego trip"), + lay on, to impose. To lay a trip on someone — to burden them with your own problems, demands, or guilt; to try to manipulate them — is late-1960s–70s counterculture slang. Its best-known descendant is guilt trip (1970s), as in "Don’t lay a guilt trip on me."
biblical_def: To lay a trip on someone is to dump your expectations, problems, or guilt on them — to pressure or manipulate them emotionally. "Don’t lay that trip on me, man." Its surviving form is the guilt trip. The Christian observation: the phrase names two different things, and Scripture treats them differently. The first is manipulation — using guilt, pressure, and emotion to get one’s way. Our Lord rebuked the religious leaders who did exactly that with rules: "they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders" (Mat 23:4). A parent, a pastor, or a friend who lays guilt trips is laying burdens God never laid. The second thing the phrase can dismiss, however, is the legitimate claim of love. When a friend says "I need your help," that is not a trip; it is the law of Christ: "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2). The counterculture often used "don’t lay a trip on me" to refuse any obligation at all. Scripture holds both truths: bear one another’s burdens, and "every man shall bear his own burden" (Gal 6:5). And over all false guilt it speaks the gospel: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1); "if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart" (1Jn 3:20). The believer neither lays guilt trips nor lives under them, because the only real guilt has been carried away by the One who bore it.
webster_summary: Late-1960s counterculture slang for burdening someone with your problems, demands, or guilt (whence guilt trip) — Scripture condemns the manipulator’s heavy burdens (Mat 23:4) but upholds bearing one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2), and frees from false guilt (Rom 8:1).
webster_full: LAY A TRIP ON, v. phr. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–70s) To impose one’s own expectations, problems, or feelings on another; to pressure or manipulate, especially by inducing guilt. Hence guilt trip (1970s); ego trip, power trip.

Webster (1828) — LAY, verb transitive 15. To asses; to charge; to impose; as, to lay a tax on land; to lay a duty on salt. 16. To charge; to impute; as, to lay blame on one; to lay want of prudence to one’s charge. 17. To impose, as evil, burden, or punishment. The Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. Isaiah 5:6 3.
Decode for families: "Mom, you’re guilt-tripping me" is this phrase in its Gen Z form.
scriptures: Mat 23:4
For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Gal 6:5
For every man shall bear his own burden.
Rom 8:1
There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things.
corruption_summary: The phrase rightly resists emotional manipulation but was often used to refuse any obligation of love; Scripture forbids laying false burdens, commands bearing one another’s burdens, and lifts false guilt in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Every family knows the guilt trip: the sigh, the reminder of all that has been sacrificed, the hint that a good son would call more often. It is a sin, because it uses love as a lever, and it usually fails, because guilt produces resentment rather than love. Our Lord saw it in its religious form — burdens laid on the people by men who would not lift a finger (Mat 23:4) — and He offered instead an easy yoke.

But the 1960s turned the phrase into a shield against every claim. A parent’s request, a friend’s need, a church’s call to duty — all could be dismissed as someone "laying a trip." Galatians 6 refuses that dismissal: bearing burdens is the law of Christ (Gal 6:2). The difference between a burden of love and a guilt trip is whether it is offered freely or extracted by pressure. A Christian family learns to ask freely, give gladly, and leave guilt where Christ left it — nailed to the cross (Rom 8:1).
roots_summary: Lay on (to impose) + mid-1960s trip (a state of mind) → late-1960s lay a trip on → 1970s guilt trip, ego trip, power trip.
roots_lines: Old English lecgan — to lay, to place; lay on — to impose (a burden, a tax)
Mid-1960s: trip — a drug experience; then any mental state or preoccupation
Late 1960s: lay a trip on — to burden or manipulate
1970s: guilt trip; ego trip; power trip
Greek baros — a burden borne for another (Gal 6:2); phortion — one’s own load (Gal 6:5)
usage: "Grandma never laid a guilt trip on anyone. She just made pie and waited."
Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ (Gal 6:2).
There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1).

etymology: Drift in the sense of the general meaning or tendency of what someone says ("the drift of his argument") is old English, given by Webster in 1828. Catch my drift? / Get my drift? — "Do you understand what I’m getting at?" — is twentieth-century American colloquial, very common in the 1950s–70s, often with a wink that means the speaker is hinting rather than saying it outright.
biblical_def: Catch my drift? means "Do you understand what I’m getting at?" It is usually said after a hint rather than a plain statement, with a raised eyebrow. The Christian observation: the phrase is a small window into two biblical concerns — understanding and plain speech. On understanding: God wants His people to catch His drift. When Ezra read the law, the Levites "read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Neh 8:8). Philip asked the Ethiopian, "Understandest thou what thou readest?" (Act 8:30). The Lord Jesus ended His parables with a summons to catch the drift: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear" (Mat 13:9), and after the resurrection "opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures" (Luk 24:45). On plain speech: Paul insists that a speaker who is not understood is wasting breath: "except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air" (1Co 14:9). The wink in catch my drift sometimes hides a meaning the speaker would not want to say plainly — an innuendo, a threat, a hint of something improper. The Christian should prefer the open word. A father can use the phrase with a smile and still teach his children that God does not speak in winks; He has made His drift plain in His Son.
webster_summary: Mid-20th-c. colloquial (on the 1828 drift, "meaning, tendency") for "Do you understand what I’m getting at?" — Scripture prizes understanding (Neh 8:8) and plain speech (1Co 14:9) over the wink.
webster_full: CATCH MY DRIFT, phr. (American colloquial, 20th c.; common 1950s–70s) Do you understand what I mean? Often used after a hint or an indirect statement. Also get my drift.
Webster (1828) — DRIFT, noun 4. Course of any thing; tendency; aim; main force; as the drift of reasoning or argument; the drift of a discourse.
Decode for families: the Gen Z equivalent is "if you know, you know" — also a hint, also worth asking about.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
Mat 13:9
Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.
Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
corruption_summary: A harmless colloquialism; its only shadow is the wink that hints at what one will not say plainly, and Scripture prefers words easy to be understood.
corruption_paragraphs: Most of the time catch my drift is simply friendly: "Are you following me?" But the phrase has a sly use too. A man hints at a bribe, an innuendo, or a threat and asks if you catch his drift, so that he can later deny having said anything. Scripture’s preference for plain speech (Mat 5:37; 1Co 14:9) cuts against that sly use. The godly man does not need a wink; he says what he means.

The phrase also reminds the Christian of his chief task as a hearer: to catch God’s drift. The Scriptures are not a code for insiders but a word given to be understood, and God gives teachers to explain it (Neh 8:8) and His Spirit to open the mind (Luk 24:45). A family that reads the Bible together and asks, "What is God getting at here?" is asking the right question.
roots_summary: Old English drifan (to drive) → drift (that which is driven; tendency, meaning; 1828) → 20th-c. colloquial catch / get my drift.
roots_lines: Old English drifan — to drive, to impel
Middle English drift — a driving; that which is driven, as snow
16th c.–: drift — the tendency or general meaning of speech (1828)
20th c.: catch my drift? / get my drift?
Greek syniēmi — to understand, to put together (Mat 13:15; Luk 24:45)
usage: "Curfew is ten, and the car is mine, not yours. Catch my drift?" "Yes, sir."
They gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading (Neh 8:8).
Who hath ears to hear, let him hear (Mat 13:9).
